messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kofi is a 33-year-old African man who works as a tailor in his community. He has been single for several years and spends most of his time focusing on his craft. On the surface, Kofi appears to be a dedicated worker, but beneath this veneer lies a complex web of trauma symptoms that have significantly impacted his life. Kofi was a victim of a terrorist attack at a local market he frequented regularly. The event left him in a state of shock and fear. He vividly recalls the chaos and panic as the attackers roamed freely through the crowd, but these memories often come with feelings of numbness, as if he were observing someone else's trauma. This sense of detachment has made it challenging for Kofi to fully process what happened. At times, entire segments of that day are shrouded in a fog of memory gaps, leaving him frustrated and anxious about the unknown details. Since the attack, Kofi has developed an intense need for control and safety, which manifests in his hypervigilant behavior. He now scans for exits as soon as he enters any room or building and feels safest when his back is against a wall where he can see everything happening around him. This constant state of alertness has become a significant part of his daily routine. The traumatic event has also deeply affected Kofi’s self-perception. He harbors doubts about his ability to make the right decisions, feeling weak and unable to trust himself. These negative appraisals have led him to seek escape through maladaptive strategies. For instance, he spends long hours on his phone playing games or browsing the internet as a way to avoid thinking about what happened. This habit has gradually increased over time, leaving him isolated from others. Kofi's tendency to pick arguments and create drama is another coping mechanism that emerged after the trauma. He finds that these conflicts distract him from the lingering fears and memories of the attack. However, this behavior has strained his relationships with colleagues and friends, further isolating him. The memory replay he experiences serves as a constant reminder of the event. These intrusive recollections often play out like a film in his mind, overwhelming him and driving him back to his maladaptive strategies for relief. The more Kofi tries to avoid these memories by engaging in distractions or conflicts, the stronger they become, creating a vicious cycle that leaves him feeling increasingly trapped. Kofi’s hypervigilance has also led him to develop additional avoidance behaviors, such as avoiding making any future plans. This fear of unpredictability and potential danger keeps him from committing to anything beyond his immediate surroundings. The more he avoids these situations, the deeper his sense of self-doubt grows, reinforcing the belief that he is weak and unable to cope. What frightens Kofi most is the possibility of another attack and the realization that he might not be able to protect himself or others. He finds himself constantly scanning for threats and feeling unsafe in public spaces, which has led him to work longer hours at his tailor shop to avoid going out. This pattern of behavior has taken a toll on both his personal life and professional relationships. Kofi's current state is one of deep distress and uncertainty. The combination of hypervigilance, memory intrusions, negative self-perceptions, and maladaptive coping strategies has created a cycle that he feels unable to break free from on his own. He finally decided to seek help when the isolation and constant fear began affecting his ability to work effectively and maintain any meaningful connections with others. Kofi hopes for support in understanding and managing these overwhelming symptoms so that he can regain control of his life and reconnect with the world around him.
